About Me

I enjoy having conversations
with people

I enjoy having conversations with people and learning about their needs.

I discovered this while interning at A&L Canada, an agricultural research company. Farmers come to us with their challenges, and we helped them identify the root cause. Through back-and-forth conversations, I learned that farmers know their fields better than anyone, and with the right questions, they guided me in uncovering the challenge.

Going back to university, I was connected to the Centre for Research on Health Equity and Social Inclusion (CRHESI) and had the opportunity to collaborate with community partners, policymakers, and people with lived experience to advance equitable practices.

I'm drawn to problems sitting at the intersection of systems thinking, communication, and equity — and I believe the best solutions come from listening deeply and designing with communities, not just for them. Now, I am looking for an exciting opportunity in service design or research 🙂

Health Equity · Research · Strategy

Health Equity · Community Research · CRHESI

Collecting Sociodemographic Data
for Equitable Change

OrganizationCRHESI, Western University
MethodsQualitative Interviews · Literature Review
Sources Reviewed40 Articles
StatusIn Progress

Overview

For this project, I worked with CRHESI to explore how health and social service organizations can collect sociodemographic data in ways that advance equity while minimizing harm. I conducted a literature review and one-on-one interviews with key informants across frontline administration, senior management, data management, and service providers. This project helped me understand that effective data collection is not just technical, but depends on trust, cultural safety, governance, and meaningful use of the data.

About CRHESI

The Centre for Research on Health Equity and Social Inclusion (CRHESI) is an interdisciplinary research initiative based at Western University's Faculty of Health Sciences. Established through a university-community partnership, CRHESI brings together researchers, students, service providers, policymakers, funders, and people with lived experience to advance health equity and social inclusion in London and surrounding communities. Its work focuses on supporting community-engaged research, building trusted partnerships, and mobilizing evidence to inform policy, service delivery, and positive social change.

Background

Sociodemographic (SD) data collection is vital for informing healthcare and social service centres on how to best serve their communities. SD data provide insights into identifying gaps for the underserved community and supporting decision-making in resource allocation for these services. As such, an Ontario mandate for SD data collection in these services was ordered in 2020.

During the data collection process, CRHESI's community partners face challenges in collecting these data not only systematically but also equitably and meaningfully. Therefore, my team and I began our research on collecting SD data for equitable change.

Problem Definition

When the project was first tasked to us, it was unclear to us why this project was needed in the first place. Isn't the data collection process straightforward? A piece of paper or a survey for clients to fill in? Isn't this process often voluntary or always consensual?

To clear this ambiguity, we took three steps to learn more about this topic:

  • Internal discussion: My teammate and I discussed what we think the problem could really be in the data collection practices based on our experiences and backgrounds. We identified a few areas where we think the problem might sit.
  • Initial Research: We did some initial research to use the literature or sources of anecdotal stories to verify whether the problems we thought of exist.
  • Validation with our project host: We compiled what we found in research and brought it back to discuss with our host, ensuring our understanding of project objectives and scope aligned with CRHESI's community partners.
Overall, we found that our primary objective was to identify any systematic barriers in achieving equitable and meaningful data collection practices and any existing best practices that address those barriers.

At this stage, we knew the barriers could be a result of poor coordination across practices or a lack of trust from the clients, and these barriers often disproportionally impact underserved communities and people who have experienced trauma and violence. Therefore, we wanted to answer these three questions:

  • What did these poor practices look like?
  • How did they impact the experience of every interest holder?
  • How might we, as CRHESI, provide guidance for the community partner to work towards the best practices for equitable changes?

Research Methods

In order to answer these questions, we needed to learn from all the involved parties about their experiences. We identified five different parties as key informants for this project:

  • Administrative staff or data collectors — This group has direct contact with clients during data collection, making their insights critical to understanding gaps and identifying best practices.
  • Senior management of the organization — This group shapes the overall data collection practice, making their insights important for understanding how the process is organized, why it operates that way, and where improvements can be made.
  • Data governance expert — This group oversees how data are managed after collection, making their insights critical for understanding privacy compliance and identifying structured practices that smaller organizations could learn from.
  • TVIC Experts — This group has experience in trauma- and violence-informed care and working with vulnerable populations, making their insights critical for building trusted, respectful, and safe data collection practices.
  • Clients — This group uses the organization's services, making their experiences essential for collecting meaningful data and creating a trustworthy, respectful environment for SD data collection.

We learned the insights from these informants through two major methods: qualitative interviews and literature review.

🗣 Qualitative Interviews

We selected one-on-one qualitative interviews because the study sought to understand participants' experiences, concerns, and practical considerations in depth, rather than produce quantitative measures. Given the sensitivity of SD data collection and its connection to trust, cultural safety, trauma-informed practice, and potential harm, interviews provided a safer and more flexible format for participants to describe their perspectives in their own words. We spoke to five informants, with each interview lasting approximately 30 to 60 minutes. The interviews were guided by a draft interview guide to ensure consistency, but remained flexible so the questions could be adapted using the laddering technique. This allows for probing deeper into key themes, motivation, and underlying assumptions.

📚 Literature Review

Ideally, we should want to learn the insights from clients through on-site observation or qualitative interviews. However, working with clients would require ethics approval that often takes a long period of time. Due to the limited time for this project, it was not feasible to do so. Therefore, we supplemented the insights from clients through a literature review. The literature review was also leveraged to contextualize, support, and challenge insights from the qualitative interviews. To conduct the review, we developed key search terms, including synonyms and alternative phrases, and combined them with Boolean operators and advanced filters. Topic-specific databases such as Scopus and PubMed were used to identify academic research, while Google Scholar and Western Libraries were used to capture grey literature and white papers. In total, 40 articles were reviewed for this project.

Outcomes & Completion Rates

Across CRHESI's learning collaborative, participating organizations showed measurable improvement in sociodemographic data completion rates between 2021/22 and 2023/24 across all four indicator categories.

Fig. 1 — Average completion rates for sociodemographic indicators, CRHESI Learning Collaborative (2021/22 vs. 2023/24). Disability showed the greatest improvement (+14.3%), with an overall increase of +8.1%.

Key Findings & Results

Data Collectors / Admin Staff

Staff often understand the value of the data but may feel uncomfortable asking sensitive questions without clear scripts, training, or a strong explanation of purpose. Staff also emphasized that data collection works best when it is integrated naturally into the workflow and when clients are clearly told that participation is voluntary and will not affect their access to care.

Senior Management

Senior management emphasized that collecting the data alone is not enough; organizations must have the capacity to analyze, report, and use the data to improve equity, service planning, and decision-making. Collaboration with other organizations and exchange of insights is also important to ensure collective actions.

Data Governance Experts

SD data collection requires clear standards for how data are defined, stored, protected, and reported. They emphasized that inconsistent categories, unclear ownership, and poor data quality can limit the usefulness of the data and create risks for clients and communities.

TVIC Experts

Clients may feel intrusive or unsafe when they do not understand why the information is being requested or how it will be used. They emphasized the importance of building trust first, using trauma- and violence-informed approaches, and making it clear that clients can decline to answer without affecting their access to services.

Clients

Clients may feel uncomfortable or unsafe sharing SD information if they do not understand why it is being collected or how it will be used. Clients may also worry that refusing to answer could affect their access to care, especially when there are power imbalances between service providers and clients.

Effective sociodemographic data collection is both a technical and relational process. While standardized tools, clear governance, privacy safeguards, and practical systems are essential, successful implementation also depends on staff confidence, leadership support, culturally safe practices, and trust with clients and communities. Client perspectives further reinforce that data collection must be voluntary, clearly explained, and responsive to client comfort and consent. Most importantly, it should not be treated as a one-time administrative task, but as an ongoing, client-centred process that supports meaningful equity-focused action.

Recommendations

🌱 Organizational Culture

SD data collection should be supported by an equity-oriented culture across the whole organization, not just by frontline staff. This means building staff awareness, confidence, and training around cultural safety, trauma- and violence-informed care, and the purpose of collecting the data.

📋 Standardizing Data Collection Protocols

Organizations need clear and consistent processes for what data are collected, how questions are asked, how consent is explained, and how information is stored and used. Standardization improves data quality, but it must still allow flexibility to follow the client's comfort and pace.

🤝 Collective Action

Organizations should not approach SD data collection in isolation. Sharing resources, learning from other agencies, and participating in communities of practice can help reduce duplication, support smaller organizations, and create more consistent equity-focused practices across the sector.

💬 Engaging in Meaningful Ways

Clients and communities should be involved as partners, not just data sources. Meaningful engagement requires deep listening, trust-building, co-developing solutions, and creating ongoing relationships that allow communities to shape how data are collected, interpreted, and used.

Learning & Reflection

Empathetic Thinking: My biggest learning takeaway from this project is the importance of approaching research and service design with empathy. SD data collection may seem like a technical or administrative process, but for clients, this can be sharing an experience that is hard to open up to others. I learned that any effective information-collecting process must begin with understanding how clients may feel in those moments, and I would bring empathetic thinking and respect to my design processes in the future.

Thinking Long-term and Creating Meaningful Change to Minimize Harm: Another takeaway for me is that collecting data or information alone doesn't bring change. There are always steps that come afterwards. Therefore, it is important to have clear governance and a plan for action to ensure that whatever is done at the current stage can bring a sustainable and meaningful impact.

What I would do differently: If I were to do this project again, I would try to include more direct client perspectives. While the literature review helped us understand client concerns, speaking directly with clients or observing data collection in practice could have provided deeper insight into how people actually experience these questions at the point of service. I would also spend more time exploring the practical implementation barriers faced by frontline staff, such as time pressure, workflow constraints, and confidence in explaining why the data are being collected.

Next steps: A next step would be to investigate how these challenges differ between larger and smaller organizations. Larger organizations may have more resources, technology, and staff capacity to standardize data collection, while smaller organizations may rely more heavily on relationships, flexibility, and limited administrative capacity. Collaborating with a few organizations to discuss the feasibility of implementing the recommendations would help test how practical they are in different settings. This could also identify what support organizations need, such as shared templates, staff training, governance guidance, or communities of practice.
